items.note: Online art platform data compare text-to-image AI adopters with matched non-adopters on novel artifact contributions (productivity versus dilution effects); no assignment; SSRN version (OpenAlex W4410233406) is the same study; same authors and platform as c149.

Within-subject experiment in which 96 university students do a scientific divergent application task under group-AI, individual-AI, and human-only group modes, with outputs scored for usefulness, originality, and quality; abstract does not say whether the order of modes was randomized; preprint OpenAlex W4412882002 is the same study.

Abstract not reachable (OpenAlex, Crossref, Semantic Scholar, Europe PMC, ScienceDirect all failed); title describes a follow-up of music students after ChatGPT-4 use on creative and analytical skills, likely an after_ai design following an earlier intervention, so the full text must confirm the comparison group, assignment, and whether creativity is scored on output.

Platform data on over 4 million artworks from more than 50,000 users track productivity, favorites, and content and visual novelty after text-to-image AI adoption; no assignment; same authors and platform as c146.

Abstract not reachable for the JEBO article or the SSRN version 10.2139/ssrn.5196748 (OpenAlex, Crossref, Semantic Scholar, Europe PMC, SSRN page all failed); title says experimental evidence on generative AI adoption in creative tasks and Holzner et al. 2025 code it as people with versus without AI, so the full text must confirm assignment, N, and outcomes.

Workshop paper not located (no DOI; OpenAlex search rate-limited, web searches failed); per the search notes, alternate uses task responses from student dyads are compared with responses from 10 generative AI models and no participant used AI.

GPT-4 product ideas are rated against ideas from laypeople and incentivized creative professionals, and GPT-4 rewrites of human ideas are rated; no participant works with AI; the search notes say a meta-analysis cites the related Marketing Science paper by Li, Castelo, Katona and Sarvary, which may be a different study.

Two designs: 20 AI systems compared with 193 university students on PIC-A creative writing games, plus a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest in which students repeat the games with ChatGPT help and fluency, flexibility, and originality are scored; the AI-assisted condition always comes second, so the within-person order is not randomized.

Several LLMs and human writers each write the same epic story, and human evaluators rate fluency, coherence, originality, humor, and style; no participant uses AI; abstract from Semantic Scholar for arXiv 2310.08433, same work as the EMNLP Findings paper.
ChatGPT-4 and humans give creative interpretations of ambiguous figures (Figural Interpretation Quest), scored for flexibility and rated creativity; no participant uses AI.
